materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool

Household-accessible route: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough. For sound or performance work, tap, clap, use spoken syllables, move a finger, or notate silently. Specialized art materials, instruments, paid software, cameras, microphones, and recording devices are optional and never affect credit.
task_brief: Critique and reflection work on design iteration. Critique and reflection: define a purpose, generate alternatives, test use, and revise through design iteration, then use observable evidence to explain or revise a learner-owned decision. Use available definitions and examples, but keep intent and scored decisions your own.
primary_task: Target for this correct session: Use error evidence to choose a different representation or strategy for design iteration, then demonstrate corrected understanding. Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of design iteration. Check, revise, or improve work about design iteration using stated success criteria. Closing evidence check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about design iteration; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. 1. Error analysis: Name the observable mismatch in earlier work without judging taste or effort. Locate it, compare it with the stated criterion, and choose the smallest useful repair. 2. Supported revision: Test the repair on a separate small study before changing the scored work. Use a different cue or representation and record what the test reveals. 3. Fresh transfer: Put the support away and make a new arrangement, passage, response, or plan. Record what the fresh evidence shows; keep the earlier attempt without penalty. Your choices remain yours: Different visual or material direction, which need to prioritize, prototype format, feedback to act on, final tradeoff choices are valid when the learner meets objective constraints and supports the result with evidence. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about design iteration, and it belongs to "Studio Techniques and Design Problems", which also covers separate topics such as drawing and observation. Close out with this check before you stop: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about design iteration; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. At grade 7 the bar is independent work with reasoning that a reader can follow without you present, plus one stated check you ran on your own result before submitting.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available for spoken reflection, explanation, or critique and scores the same. Use a written analysis, labelled plan, evidence table, notation, diagram, or private artifact check that preserves the stated target. No microphone, camera, recording, or public audience is required.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Provide a non-performance or low-audience option when needed without lowering the academic target.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting design iteration.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Route 1: Reduce design iteration to three locatable events, areas, steps, or decisions. Label the intended effect beside each and underline the one purpose relationship that should carry it. Use a separate small study, four-event loop, thumbnail, evidence table, or paper plan. The adult may model the noticing process on different material but may not change the learner’s work. Check yourself: Point to or name the exact purpose evidence before deciding whether it serves the intent. New attempt: Put the support away and make a new arrangement, passage, response, or plan; record what the new evidence shows. Route 2: Return to the last understandable state. Hold every relationship steady except one chosen feature from purpose, audience need, hierarchy, legibility, constraints, feedback, and iteration; predict what that single change should do. Test the feature on scrap paper, a silent count, a two-event rehearsal loop, movable shapes, or a short evidence sentence before changing the scored work. Check yourself: Name what stayed the same, what changed, and the first observable result—without using “better” as the evidence. New attempt: Create a different small case using the same one-variable method, then transfer the finding to the original task only if it serves the learner’s intent.
extension: Apply design iteration under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on design iteration rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.

concept_instruction.title: What design iteration means here
concept_instruction.body: Design organizes choices to serve a stated purpose under real constraints.

concept_instruction.title: How the relationship changes the result
concept_instruction.body: A brief turns a need into testable criteria; contrasting sketches expose tradeoffs before time is spent refining one direction.

concept_instruction.title: Choice and tradeoff
concept_instruction.body: A solution can maximize speed, clarity, expression, access, or cost, but rarely all at once. A strong rationale names what was prioritized and why. Worked example: Two wayfinding drafts can use the same words but different hierarchy; a five-second find test reveals which supports the stated route. Non-example: Choosing the most polished draft without checking it against the brief treats taste as evidence.

technique_sequence.action: State the intended effect or question before making or judging.
technique_sequence.notice: The statement creates a criterion that can be checked.
technique_sequence.why: Arts evidence is interpreted in relation to purpose, not personal taste.

technique_sequence.action: Identify or set up the relevant purpose, audience need, hierarchy, legibility, constraints, feedback, and iteration.
technique_sequence.notice: Locate the first relationship that can be observed in design iteration.
technique_sequence.why: A brief turns a need into testable criteria; contrasting sketches expose tradeoffs before time is spent refining one direction.

technique_sequence.action: Complete one small controlled study or rehearsal loop.
technique_sequence.notice: Keep most relationships stable so one decision remains readable.
technique_sequence.why: A bounded test makes cause and effect easier to notice.

technique_sequence.action: Transfer the idea to a fresh work, excerpt, source detail, or project decision.
technique_sequence.notice: Close the model or cue before the independent decision.

technique_sequence.action: Check against criteria and choose a revision or a reasoned decision to keep the result.
technique_sequence.notice: Cite a location, moment, event, or process fact before judging.
technique_sequence.why: Evidence protects creative variation and learner authority.

common_technique_errors.observable_mismatch: The stated intent for design iteration is present, but the record does not yet locate purpose, audience need, hierarchy, legibility, constraints, feedback, and iteration that supports it.
common_technique_errors.not_an_error_when: The learner supports a different, ambiguous, subtle, or intentionally open effect with observable evidence.

common_technique_errors.observable_mismatch: Several relationships changed at once, so the learner cannot yet tell which choice caused the observed effect.
common_technique_errors.not_an_error_when: The task is an intentionally exploratory diagnostic and no causal claim is being scored.
